Risk & Issue Management.q: A supplier misses a key delivery. The project manager records it and assigns it to the procurement lead. What stage of the issue resolution process is this?
Risk & Issue Management.w: The issue has been logged and assigned to a responsible owner — a key early step in resolution.

n.1: Escalation only occurs if the issue cannot be resolved internally.
n.0: The issue hasn’t been resolved yet.
n.2: Resolution comes after assignment.
n.4: Stakeholder engagement may occur later.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following best defines a 'risk' in project management?
o: A confirmed problem that must be resolved immediately
A failure to meet a milestone deadline
An uncertain event that, if it occurs, may impact project objectives
A cost overrun that cannot be avoided
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk is an uncertain event that may have a positive or negative impact on the project.

n.0: This describes an issue, not a risk.
n.4: A cost overrun is typically a realised issue.
n.1: Missing a milestone is an outcome, not a potential risk.
n.2: Completed tasks are not uncertain events.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A risk management plan identifies that poor weather may delay construction. What benefit does this provide?
o: It allows the team to create mitigation plans before delays occur
It avoids the need for configuration control
It guarantees the project stays within scope
It removes the impact of all environmental risks
It triggers procurement of new equipment immediately
Risk & Issue Management.w: Proactively identifying risks gives the team time to develop responses before issues arise.

n.1: Configuration control is still needed regardless of risk plans.
n.3: Not all environmental risks can be avoided — only mitigated.
n.2: Scope control is separate from risk planning.
n.4: Procurement is only triggered by specific planned actions, not every identified risk.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A supplier fails to deliver components on time, affecting the project schedule. What is the role of issue management in this situation?
o: Change the scope to remove the affected tasks
Escalate the delay as a risk
Document the issue, assign ownership, and track resolution
Risk & Issue Management.w: Issue management tracks real disruptions like missed deliveries, ensuring they are handled and closed out.

n.2: The delay has already occurred — it's an issue, not a risk.
n.4: Phase planning is unrelated to resolving current issues.
n.1: Scope changes must be justified — not an automatic response.
n.0: Unmanaged delays can damage delivery — they must be addressed.

Risk & Issue Management.q: At what point in the issue resolution process is ownership formally assigned?
Risk & Issue Management.w: After logging the issue, ownership should be promptly assigned to ensure timely resolution.

n.4: By closure, the issue has already been resolved.
n.1: Analysis often involves the assigned owner.
n.3: Escalation may follow assignment, not replace it.
n.0: Identification precedes assignment but does not include it.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the purpose of developing a risk response plan?
o: To assign actions that reduce, avoid, transfer, or accept risks
To replace the stakeholder engagement plan
To develop a work breakdown structure
To document the acceptance criteria for final deliverables
To define how the team will react when issues are logged
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risk response plans outline what actions will be taken for each risk — including reduction, avoidance, transfer or acceptance.

n.4: Issue management is separate from risk response.
n.3: Acceptance criteria are part of quality or scope planning.
n.1: Stakeholder engagement is a different knowledge area.
n.2: WBS supports scope, not risk management.

Risk & Issue Management.q: When should a project risk be formally closed?
o: When it is no longer relevant or has been addressed
When it has been transferred to a third party
Risk & Issue Management.w: A risk is closed when it is no longer a threat or opportunity, either due to mitigation or expiry.

n.2: Risks emerge throughout the project, not just at initiation.
n.4: Risk closure can occur during the project, not only at the end.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What happens during the closure stage of issue management?
o: Formal verification and sign-off that the issue is resolved
Risk & Issue Management.w: Closure confirms that the issue is resolved and that all necessary documentation is complete.

n.2: Logging is the first step — not closure.
n.4: Assignment occurs early in the process.
n.1: Resolution happens before closure.
n.0: Estimating impact happens during analysis, not closure.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following best describes the timing of an issue compared to a risk?
o: An issue is tracked in the risk register
An issue is a past or current event, while a risk is a future possibility
An issue is resolved before a project begins
An issue is more severe than a risk

n.3: Issues can arise at any stage, not just before the project.
n.4: Severity depends on impact, not classification.
n.1: Issues are tracked separately from risks.
n.0: Not all issues require escalation — many are resolved at the project level.

Risk & Issue Management.q: What is the primary reason risks and issues are tracked separately?
o: They follow different lifecycle stages and require separate treatment
Issues must be resolved before project start
Risk tracking is optional; issue tracking is mandatory
They are managed by different teams
Risk & Issue Management.w: Risks are analysed and planned for; issues are resolved as they occur — so they need different processes.

n.2: Both risks and issues can be escalated.
n.4: The same team can manage both.
n.1: Issues arise at any point — not just before the project starts.
n.3: Both risk and issue tracking are important and expected.

Risk & Issue Management.q: During testing, a defect is discovered that prevents deployment. What is this?

n.4: Schedule buffers absorb delays, not defects.
n.3: Baselines are planned values — unrelated to test results.
n.2: Assumptions are expectations, not events.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following is typically recorded during the issue resolution closure stage?
o: The date the issue was resolved and actions taken
The potential likelihood of the issue
Risk & Issue Management.w: Closure should include the resolution date and a summary of actions taken to address the issue.

n.3: RACI applies to roles/responsibilities, not directly to issue closure.
n.1: This relates to the risk that may have become the issue, not the issue itself.
n.4: Escalation is addressed earlier if needed, not at closure.

Risk & Issue Management.q: Which of the following is NOT typically part of the issue management process?
o: Scoring the issue’s probability and impact
Logging the issue in a formal register
Assigning an owner to the issue
Risk & Issue Management.w: Scoring likelihood and impact is part of risk management, not issue management — issues have already occurred.

n.2: Issues are logged formally for tracking and resolution.
n.3: Each issue should have an owner responsible for action.
n.4: Progress tracking ensures resolution is followed through.
n.1: Formal closure confirms the issue has been resolved.

Risk & Issue Management.q: A stakeholder demands that an issue be escalated before any assessment is made. What should the project manager do?

Assign it to a team member without logging
Risk & Issue Management.w: Escalation should follow internal assessment to decide if the issue exceeds project authority.

n.3: Escalation without assessment may be unnecessary.
n.4: The issue must be addressed, not closed prematurely.
n.1: Stakeholder input is important, but procedure must be followed.
n.2: Issues should always be logged before being assigned.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following best describes the responsibility of a project team member?

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A development team is waiting on the next batch of prioritised work. Who is responsible for ensuring the backlog is updated and properly ordered?

Roles & Responsibilities.q: An IT system has been implemented and early feedback shows that users are confused by some of the interface language. What project action best supports successful adoption?

Roles & Responsibilities.q: What distinguishes the PMO from a project manager?

n.1: Roles are clearly defined.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: You’ve been assigned to a new IT project as a business analyst. Your tasks include gathering requirements, attending progress meetings, and supporting testing. What role are you performing?

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following tasks would typically fall *outside* the project manager’s responsibilities?

Communicating with the project team and stakeholders

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A product owner decides to delay development of a planned feature in favour of a new feature requested by customers. What does this decision demonstrate?

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following is a key responsibility of the project sponsor?

n.0: End users are the recipients of project outputs.

n.4: Backlog management is the product owner's responsibility.

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A project manager requests a standard risk register template and guidance on preparing for a gateway review. Which project role typically provides these support services?

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A team member fails to deliver a critical task on time, affecting the project’s schedule. What is the project manager’s most appropriate response?

Assign the task to the governance board
Discuss the issue, identify root causes, and support resolution
Immediately escalate to the sponsor for dismissal
Ignore it and adjust the project deadline

Roles & Responsibilities.q: The sponsor has asked for a status report on progress and risk. What should the project manager include in the report?

Benefit realisation updates and post-project audits
Updates on schedule, budget, risks, and key deliverables
User feedback analysis from closed change initiatives

To justify staff changes within delivery teams

Roles & Responsibilities.q: You’ve just identified a critical delay due to a late supplier delivery. What is the most appropriate action for the project manager to take first?

Cancel team meetings until the supplier issue is resolved
Notify procurement that the project will be cancelled
Reassign the project to the product owner

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A sponsor has just signed off the project business case and committed the funding. What should be their next priority?

Roles & Responsibilities.q: You are managing a digital project using agile delivery. A stakeholder is responsible for maintaining the product backlog and prioritising which features are developed next. What role is this person performing?

Roles & Responsibilities.q: Which of the following is a core responsibility of the project manager?

Roles & Responsibilities.q: You are leading a complex infrastructure project with multiple suppliers and stakeholders. You are responsible for managing day-to-day activities, controlling risks, and ensuring deliverables are completed on time. What role are you fulfilling?

Roles & Responsibilities.q: A PMO analyst notices that three projects across the portfolio are reporting schedule delays and inconsistent risk reporting. What action should the PMO take?

Project Management & Operating Environme.w: A project is a temporary endeavour with a defined beginning and end, created to deliver specific objectives.

n.1: This defines business as usual, not a project.
n.3: Customer support is a function, not a project.
n.2: Permanent departments are not temporary initiatives.
n.4: Risk mitigation may be part of a project, but does not define one.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following is *not* a characteristic of a project?
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Projects use temporary teams and resources tailored for the specific objective.

n.1: Projects deliver something unique.
n.3: Projects always have a start and finish.
n.2: Projects exist to meet specific goals.
n.4: Projects are not ongoing operations.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: You are managing a project to deliver a new performance appraisal system. It must be handed over to the HR department within 6 weeks. o: The HR department has more budgetary control.
The project is focused on stakeholder engagement.
The HR team also handles documentation and delivery.
The project has a defined end date and unique output.
The project supports daily operational routines.

n.1: Stakeholder engagement applies to both.
n.0: Budget control isn’t the defining difference.
n.2: This doesn't illustrate the temporary nature of a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A project sponsor is concerned about high inflation and interest rate changes impacting a capital investment project. Which category of PESTLE should be examined?
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Economic factors such as inflation and interest rates directly influence project viability and costs.

n.3: Legal factors relate to laws, not economic trends.
n.0: Environmental relates to physical and ecological conditions.
n.2: Technology refers to systems, tools, and innovation.
n.1: Sociological relates to demographics or culture.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A retail organisation is running a series of related projects to implement online ordering, mobile app development, and supply chain automation. What type of management ensures these projects are aligned for maximum benefit?
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Programme management coordinates related projects to achieve greater combined benefits than if managed separately.

n.0: Portfolio management oversees all change initiatives, not just related projects.
n.4: Quality assurance ensures deliverables meet requirements.
n.1: Stakeholder management is a supporting discipline, not a grouping mechanism.
n.2: Change control manages scope within a project.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: You are planning a major event-based project in a city centre. The council warns of increased scrutiny due to local air quality regulations. Which part of PESTLE does this most relate to?
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Environmental factors include sustainability, pollution, and compliance with ecological regulations.

n.2: Political relates to government actions but not specifically air quality.
n.0: Legal relates to laws; air quality is more of an environmental concern here.
n.1: Technology is unrelated to the regulation in question.
n.3: Sociological factors focus on human behaviour and demographics.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: Which of the following best summarises the key purpose of project management?
o: To help organisations respond to change and deliver specific objectives
To increase headcount in operational areas
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Project management allows organisations to deliver change and meet specific time, cost and quality objectives.

n.4: Reporting is useful but not the core purpose.
n.3: Project management complements BAU, it does not replace it.
n.2: Increasing staff is a result, not a project management goal.
n.0: Cost tracking is a function, not the purpose.

Project Management & Operating Environme.q: A new CEO is reviewing all change initiatives and decides to cancel two projects, start three new ones, and combine a group of related initiatives under one business programme. Which type of management is the CEO applying?
Project Management & Operating Environme.w: Portfolio management includes prioritising, terminating or initiating projects based on strategic alignment.

n.1: Change control applies to project scope, not strategic direction.
n.3: Project management handles delivery, not strategic selection.
n.4: Programme assurance focuses on execution, not selection.
n.0: Operational leadership may guide BAU, but this is clearly portfolio management.

Life Cycles.q: A project to install new manufacturing equipment is using a linear life cycle. The equipment is delivered and installed, and staff are trained to use it. Which phase is most likely being completed?
Life Cycles.w: The Handover and Closure phase involves transitioning deliverables to users and closing the project.

n.3: Concept phase is for initial justification.

Life Cycles.q: Your client wants a clear upfront cost and schedule for deployment, but also wants to experiment with features after go-live. Which life cycle approach is most suitable?
Life Cycles.w: A hybrid model allows a fixed deployment plan with flexibility for feature evolution through iterative methods.

n.1: Iterative doesn’t provide fixed upfront planning.
n.3: Linear would not accommodate changes well.
n.0: Extended covers post-project activities, not development models.
n.4: RAD is a fast iterative approach, not a structured hybrid.

Life Cycles.q: Your team is developing a new mobile app using short development cycles and regular feedback sessions with end users. Which project life cycle are you most likely following?
Life Cycles.w: An iterative life cycle delivers in small increments and refines the product through regular stakeholder feedback.

n.4: Linear life cycles deliver in a single pass after upfront planning.
n.3: Extended refers to including post-project phases.
n.0: Hybrid combines elements of linear and iterative.
n.2: Waterfall is another name for linear delivery.

Life Cycles.q: Which of the following best describes a core feature of an iterative life cycle?
o: Complete scope is defined upfront and delivered once
There are no formal reviews during delivery
Benefits are realised after final delivery only
The product is released in small increments with frequent reassessment
Change control is discouraged throughout the process
Life Cycles.w: Iterative life cycles focus on releasing product increments and adjusting based on feedback.

n.0: This describes a linear life cycle.
n.2: Iterative approaches aim for early and frequent benefit delivery.
n.1: Reviews are essential in iterative models.
n.4: Iterative delivery encourages adaptive planning and managed change.

Life Cycles.q: A project manager is coordinating a system upgrade. The infrastructure is delivered using a linear model, while customer-facing features are developed and adjusted during delivery. What is the term for this delivery model?
Life Cycles.w: This describes a hybrid life cycle – mixing sequential and iterative components depending on the work type.

n.1: Parallel projects run concurrently but are not necessarily integrated in delivery method.
n.0: Agile focuses on iterative delivery throughout.
n.3: Waterfall is a purely linear life cycle.
n.2: Extended refers to post-project activities, not life cycle integration.

Life Cycles.q: You are managing a construction project using a linear life cycle. The requirements are fully defined at the start. What is the correct sequence of phases you will follow?
o: Concept, Definition, Development, Handover and Closure
Life Cycles.w: A typical linear life cycle includes: Concept, Definition, Development, Handover and Closure.

n.0: Feasibility is not one of the standard four phases in a linear life cycle.

n.2: These terms do not align with the APM standard linear cycle.
n.4: This structure doesn't reflect APM guidance.

Life Cycles.q: Which of the following would be a key reason to adopt a hybrid life cycle?
o: The product is simple and repetitive
The customer has minimal involvement in delivery
All requirements are fixed and well understood
Parts of the project are predictable, but other parts require flexibility
Life Cycles.w: Hybrid approaches are ideal when some components need rigid control and others benefit from adaptive delivery.

n.3: Fully fixed requirements suit a linear model.
n.2: Hybrid and iterative models often need strong customer engagement.
n.0: Simple, repeatable products fit linear delivery.
n.1: Project governance is important regardless of life cycle.

Life Cycles.q: Which activity typically occurs during the Concept phase of a linear life cycle?
o: Allocating detailed tasks to team members
Defining the business need and case for change

Life Cycles.q: Your development team has completed three product iterations, each adding new functionality based on stakeholder input. This delivery model is best suited for what type of requirement environment?
Life Cycles.w: Iterative life cycles are well suited to evolving or unclear requirements that benefit from feedback-driven development.

n.4: Stable requirements typically suit a linear life cycle.
n.0: If requirements are fixed, there's less need for iteration.
n.2: Legal constraints may still be present, but this isn't about adaptability.
n.1: Outsourced packages are typically fixed scope and schedule.

Life Cycles.q: What is the primary purpose of the extended project life cycle?
o: To reduce resource usage during development
To manage post-project benefits and performance
Life Cycles.w: The extended life cycle ensures that benefits are realised and performance monitored after handover.

n.0: It focuses on post-delivery activity, not time reduction.
n.2: Planning occurs earlier in the cycle.
n.4: Stakeholder involvement may still be needed.
n.1: Resource reduction is not the main goal.

Life Cycles.q: Which of the following best describes a hybrid life cycle?
o: A life cycle used only in construction projects
A version of the extended life cycle with additional benefits
A combination of linear and iterative life cycle elements
An adaptive model that only uses agile techniques
A sequence of fixed scope deliveries with no overlap
Life Cycles.w: Hybrid life cycles combine aspects of both linear (predictive) and iterative (adaptive) approaches to meet project needs.

n.4: This describes a purely linear approach.
n.3: Agile is just one form of iterative delivery, not hybrid.
n.1: Extended refers to post-project benefit management.
n.0: Hybrid approaches are used in multiple industries, not just construction.

Life Cycles.q: You are managing a software implementation where infrastructure must be installed in a fixed order, but software features will be released in cycles based on user feedback. What type of life cycle are you using?
Life Cycles.w: A hybrid life cycle combines elements of both linear and iterative approaches, like fixed infrastructure followed by agile software delivery.

n.3: Linear applies only when the entire scope is fixed and delivered sequentially.
n.0: Iterative would not include fixed sequential dependencies.
n.1: Extended refers to post-project activities, not delivery models.
n.4: Incremental refers to delivery in pieces but not necessarily with iteration.

Life Cycles.q: In an iterative life cycle, what typically happens after each development iteration?
o: All risks are transferred to suppliers
Stakeholder feedback is gathered and used to adjust future development
The final product is closed and signed off

n.2: Final sign-off happens at project closure, not after each iteration.
n.4: The business case is usually reviewed periodically, not rewritten every iteration.
n.3: The team continues through the project unless restructuring occurs.
n.0: Risk management is ongoing; not all risks are outsourced.

Life Cycles.q: In a typical linear life cycle, what is the main purpose of the Closure phase?

n.3: The business case is usually approved during Concept or Definition.
n.0: Design is completed earlier in the cycle.
n.4: Build happens in the Development phase.
n.1: Training typically takes place during Handover.

Life Cycles.q: You are planning a project using a linear life cycle. At which phase would the detailed schedule and budget typically be finalised?
Life Cycles.w: The Definition phase involves developing detailed plans, budgets and schedules.

n.1: The Concept phase is for early scoping and feasibility.
n.2: Development is where the actual work takes place.
n.3: Handover is about transferring deliverables.
n.4: Closure is focused on final evaluation and lessons learned.

Life Cycles.q: You are closing a project that delivered a new CRM system. However, you are also required to monitor how well the new system is used and whether it delivers the expected benefits. What part of the life cycle does this activity belong to?
Life Cycles.w: Activities like benefit realisation and performance monitoring after delivery are part of the extended life cycle.

n.4: Development focuses on building the product or service.
n.0: Definition is about planning and detailing scope, cost and time.

n.3: The standard linear cycle does not include post-delivery benefit management.

Life Cycles.q: Which of the following is most associated with the extended project life cycle?
Life Cycles.w: Extended life cycles focus on benefit tracking, often long after handover has occurred.

n.4: Requirement identification happens during early planning phases.
n.2: WBS is part of detailed planning.
n.0: Task allocation occurs during execution.
n.1: Procurement is typically done during planning and development.

Life Cycles.q: After project closure, the sponsor requests periodic reviews to measure whether the anticipated return on investment is being achieved. What does this indicate?

That extended life cycle activities are underway

Life Cycles.q: Your project team has handed over a new document management system to the operational team. What activity would typically follow in the extended project life cycle?
o: Evaluating actual benefits achieved compared to those forecast
Running performance tests on the old system
